Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 48 min read (9503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~48 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1.
  • It has been revealed that integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research.
  • However, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing1. Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses2. Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms3,4,5. However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

It has been revealed that integrated photonic devices have emerged as a powerful platform for the next-generation information technologies, and the development of efficient and scalable integrated photonic circuits has become a central focus of state-of-the-art research. Photonics enables ultrafast signal propagation, low-loss transport, broadband modulation and highly efficient information processing6,7. In this context, it is crucial that the same architecture supports a variety of integrated components, including on-chip coherent light sources, frequency-comb generators, modulators, amplifiers and switches, enabling coherent phase manipulation of propagating optical fields as a key functionality for dynamical reconfigurability and interferometric-based operations.

However, the effectiveness of all-optical devices depends critically on the ability to harness optical nonlinearities. As conventional platforms based on linear dielectric materials or lithium niobate (LiNbO3) show intrinsically weak nonlinear responses8,9, structures supporting exciton–polaritons have been proposed as an effective alternative. These hybrid light–matter excitations, formed under non-perturbative radiation coupling between excitons and purely photonic eigenmodes, combine photon-like propagation with strong optical nonlinearities, making them attractive for ultrafast all-optical information processing10,11,12,13. Although exciton–polaritons have been extensively studied in vertically confined microcavities, planar architectures such as polariton waveguides14,15,16,17 have recently attracted increasing interest owing to their ability to confine light within smaller modal volumes, thereby enhancing exciton–photon coupling, increasing polariton group velocities and facilitating on-chip integration. When combined with suitable active materials showing large exciton binding energies, polariton operation can be sustained at room temperature5, a condition fulfilled by perovskites, which stand out for their exceptional and tunable optoelectronic properties and ease of processing, eliminating the demanding fabrication procedures typically required for conventional semiconductors. In addition, their strong polariton nonlinearities, comparable to that of gallium arsenide (GaAs)-based systems, makes them an increasingly attractive platform for polariton-based applications at room temperature18,19,20,21. However, fabricating high-quality perovskite photonic components remains challenging because well-defined edges and smooth surfaces are essential for achieving satisfactory performance22,23,24, whereas conventional postprocessing often degrades the crystal morphology and optical quality. Despite recent progress, efficient in-coupling and out-coupling of light remains a main bottleneck. In particular, the realization of coherent on-chip tunable light sources, optical amplification of propagating polariton signals and efficient nonlinear phase control—only partially explored in planar microcavities under cryogenic conditions25 and still absent in guided propagating polariton systems—remains a key outstanding challenge. Overcoming these limitations is crucial to achieving robust, room-temperature, scalable and fully integrated nonlinear photonic devices.

Here we address these critical challenges by developing a fully integrated perovskite-based polaritonic circuit in which waveguides and grating couplers are simultaneously defined within the active materials using an innovative bottom-up soft-lithographic strategy that combines surface-tension-assisted and microfluidic growth processes26,27,28. This growth approach eliminates the need for any subsequent postprocessing, enabling the direct integration of hundreds-of-micrometres-long, micrometre-wide caesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3) waveguides with subwavelength gratings featuring tunable periodicity and filling factors. Under off-resonant pumping, the integrated gratings provide longitudinal optical feedback, enabling polariton lasing in an in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavity, with emission efficiently propagating along the waveguide and readily tunable by means of the grating geometry. We also demonstrate efficient optical amplification in a two-beam experiment, in which a resonantly injected propagating polariton wavepacket is amplified through stimulation from the exciton reservoir created by an extra off-resonant beam. The threshold-like amplification resembles key features of spiking neurons, offering a promising route towards the development of neuromorphic polariton devices29,30. In parallel, we achieve nonlinear optical phase control of propagating polariton signals, enabling interferometric functionalities with phase shifts reaching 2π. Our results demonstrate room-temperature polaritonic circuits with active nonlinear functionalities, marking an important step towards ultra-compact, highly nonlinear polariton devices for integrated photonics and optical information processing.

In a recent development, csPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with various geometries were directly fabricated on glass substrates using a modified soft-lithography approach that combines surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing from a liquid precursor solution, following the procedure sketched in Fig. 1a and detailed in the Methods (Supplementary Figs. 1–4). The process uses a patterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) replica moulded from a silicon master (Fig. 1b), yielding the perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings shown in Fig. 1c–e. This hybrid method enables the direct formation of hierarchical architectures through controlled self-assembly under saturation conditions and controlled temperature, yielding micrometre-scale waveguides decorated with integrated nanometric grating arrays. The soft-lithography route overcomes key limitations of conventional fabrication by exploiting elastomeric replication, enabling a simple, low-temperature and non-destructive process. It eliminates the need for multi-step lithography, avoids postprocessing damages and refractive-index mismatches, while significantly reducing fabrication cost and time.

It has been revealed that a, Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of CsPbBr3 waveguides by means of microfluidic surface-tension-driven lithography. The process follows three main steps: (1) replica moulding in PDMS of the waveguide master (left); (2) capillary-driven distribution of the precursor solution along the microstructured channels under saturated conditions and controlled temperature (centre) and (3) formation of CsPbBr3 microcrystals with the desired morphology and integrated nanometric optical gratings (right). b, Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of representative waveguides with integrated optical gratings fabricated on the silicon master through electron-beam lithography (EBL). c, Confocal images of CsPbBr3 perovskite waveguides with integrated gratings produced by the modified single-step soft-lithography technique described in a. Its features reproduce closely those fabricated in the master. d, SEM image showing a complete grating coupler directly replicated onto the CsPbBr3 perovskite structure. Right inset highlights high-resolution view of the grating from the white region in the left panel. e, High-resolution atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurement of a representative grating. f, TE-pol momentum-space photoluminescence map from one of the waveguide gratings. Here β denotes the waveguide momentum, related to the measured outcoupled wavevector by β = k ± 2π/a, where a is the grating pitch. For this specific grating, the pitch was measured to be 240 nm. Two polariton modes (yellow solid lines) are visible and marked as LP0 and LP1, respectively. The two polariton modes arise from strong coupling between two photonic modes (TE0 and TE1, white dashed lines) and the excitonic resonance. Right panel, real-space photoluminescence image of the waveguide in which the emission from several adjacent gratings is visible; the pumping spot is outside from the image in the top part. LP, lower polariton; TE-pol, TE-polarized. Scale bars, 10 μm (b,c,f); 2 μm (d).

To investigate the optical properties of the fabricated structures, we performed momentum-resolved photoluminescence and reflectivity measurements (Methods). The corresponding maps for both transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) polarizations and different pitches are shown in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. The momentum-resolved photoluminescence, obtained by spatially selecting the emission from one grating, is shown in Fig. 1f for TE polarization. Two strongly coupled modes are clearly visible (yellow solid lines), which we attribute to the fundamental (TE0) and first-order (TE1) lower polariton waveguide modes. Although the upper polariton branch is not visible31,32,33, the characteristic dispersion of the waveguide modes, which is approximated as linear in the weak coupling regime (white dashed lines), shows an increasing bending approaching the exciton resonance, providing clear evidence of the strong radiation-matter coupling. Reflectivity and photoluminescence data were fitted using a two-coupled-oscillator model yielding Rabi splitting energies of Ω = 140 ± 10 meV for both the TE1 and TE0 modes (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6), consistent with previous reports23,34. The presence of these two modes is compatible with a waveguide thickness ranging between 250 nm and 290 nm, as confirmed by finite-difference time-domain simulations presented in Extended Data Fig. 1 for different grating pitches. It is crucial to note that the TE1 mode appears brighter because one of its electric-field maxima lies closer to the top surface of the waveguide, where the grating is patterned, resulting in more efficient coupling to free-space radiation and a larger momentum-space linewidth. The typical real-space photoluminescence emission is shown in the right part of Fig. 1f and the exciton/photon fraction for LPB1 is reported in Supplementary Fig. 8.

In the absence of external optical resonators, lasing in perovskite microstructures can arise from optical feedback provided by sharp crystal facets acting as Fabry–Pérot cavities.23,24,35,36. In waveguide geometries, this feedback occurs predominantly in the transverse direction23, thus proving ineffective for photonic integrated circuits, which normally demand longitudinal propagation. Moreover, this lasing emission lacks spectral tunability, as it is governed by the intrinsic balance between optical gain and loss within the material. Alternative strategies based on isolated perovskite blocks evanescently coupled to active waveguides24 can promote in-plane propagation, but are limited by weak field overlap and inefficient coupling. Longitudinal polariton lasing assisted by integrated grating reflectors was demonstrated in a GaAs-based waveguide at cryogenic temperature17 and in gallium nitride (GaN)-based waveguide at room temperature37. However, in these systems the lasing mode remains confined within the reflective elements, without efficiently coupling into a propagating waveguide mode. By contrast, our approach integrates tunable lasing emission within a guided architecture, providing a direct route towards integrated polaritonic circuits. Moreover, it is achieved through a simple, scalable growth process yielding waveguides with embedded couplers, unlike the more complex fabrication required for GaAs or GaN platforms.

It has been revealed that to verify the formation of such a longitudinal optical feedback, the perovskite waveguide was off-resonantly pumped between two couplers. The real-space TE-polarized photoluminescence maps at excitation powers (P) below (left) and above (right) the lasing threshold (Pth) are shown in Fig. 2a. At low pumping power, the two outcouplers are barely visible, as only a relatively small portion of the emitted light is effectively coupled into the waveguide modes. By contrast, at high excitation power, a pronounced signal emerges from both outcouplers, suggesting that a longitudinal feedback is taking place. Notably, the lasing signal extracted from the grating disappears in TM polarization (Supplementary Fig. 9), confirming the polarization sensitivity of the feedback mechanism. To further investigate the onset and evolution of the lasing emission, we performed a real-space energy-resolved measurement and evaluated the emitted intensity (Extended Data Fig. 2) collected from one of the two outcouplers for the lasing signal (integrated between 2.31 eV and 2.32 eV), as shown in Fig. 2b. A clear threshold is observed at roughly Pth = 55 µJ cm−2, consistent with previous reports on similar perovskite materials19,35,38,39. The transition is accompanied by a clear linewidth narrowing as reported in the inset. The energy-resolved momentum-space maps are shown in Fig. 2c for the below-threshold (left panel) and above-threshold (right panel) regimes, and the corresponding kx–ky maps are reported in Supplementary Fig. 10.

Sources indicate that a, Real-space image of a Fabry–Pérot in-plane cavity formed by two gratings (highlighted by the dashed squares); below threshold (left) the emission is dominated by exciton recombination under the pump spot, whereas above threshold (right) the lasing mechanism takes place and the emission from the two gratings is stronger than the photoluminescence not coupled to the guided mode. b, Emitted intensity integrated at the grating position from real-space energy-resolved measurements as a function of pumping fluence. Data points are obtained from three consecutive power-dependence measurements performed on the same structure as shown in blue, green and orange dots. The black points represent the average of the three power-dependence measurements. Dashed black lines are guides for the eye. The inset reveals the linewidth below (black line) and above threshold (red line) obtained from energy-resolved momentum-space measurements. c, Corresponding energy-resolved momentum-space emission below (left) and above threshold (right). The white dashed lines indicate the TE0 and TE1 polariton modes propagating downward (dashed lines) and upward (solid line). d, Lasing emission from three different cavities formed by couples of gratings having different pitches (270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, respectively); when the pitch is modified the energy of the lasing energy shifts. Scale bars, 5 μm.

Lasing occurs where longitudinal feedback selects a single mode due to the balance between gain and losses taking place at the reflectivity maximum induced by the grating, where losses are minimal. This point38,40 is slightly red-shifted and momentum-shifted with respect to the bandgap because finite-size and thickness variation in the grating profile cause new loss-favoured grating-to-waveguide backreflections15, as discussed in Supplementary Fig. 11. Lasing modes show a clear blueshift with increasing power, and more Fabry–Pérot modes emerge within the same spectral region (Extended Data Fig. 3). Notably, our configuration does not rely on large reflectivity or a strongly developed stop band; rather, a small but finite reflectivity is sufficient to enable cavity formation and mode selection, owing to the excellent gain properties of CsPbBr3. To demonstrate the spectral tunability of the lasing emission, we have tuned the periodicity within the integrated couplers by keeping their mutual distance constant. As shown in Fig. 2d, for three different grating geometries with pitches of 270 nm, 260 nm and 250 nm, a progressive blueshift is induced from roughly 2.28 eV to 2.315 eV. The below-threshold and above-threshold dispersions for all the measured gratings are reported in Extended Data Fig. 4. It is vital to note that in the present device geometry, longitudinal feedback from the grating couplers coexist with transverse feedback from the waveguide edges. Above-threshold spatially resolved measurements confirm this coexistence, showing a roughly doubled mode spacing for edge emission, consistent with two cavity lengths of roughly 25 μm and 10 μm, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 12). Efficient propagation of the lasing signal along the waveguide allows its collection from the first outcoupler next to the grating-pair cavity element (Extended Data Fig. 6). From these data, together with further resonant propagation measurements, we estimate propagation losses, outcoupler attenuation and optical gain (Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14).

Sources indicate that in the following section we demonstrate another key functionality of our system: the optical amplification, which has not been previously achieved in similar polaritonic platforms at room temperature. This is essential for integrated photonic circuits as it compensates for propagation and coupling losses, thus enabling efficient on-chip light transport. We resonantly injected a pulsed beam (signal) through the input grating on the LPB1 mode and monitored the transmitted signal at the output located 25 µm away. A second pulsed beam (amplifier) was off-resonantly exciting the centre of the waveguide between two outcouplers where it generates an incoherent exciton population, as schematically shown in Fig. 3a. The signal beam was kept in the linear regime, thereby avoiding self-phase-modulation effects41 (Supplementary Fig. 15). We recorded the output intensity by scanning the time delay between the two pulses, keeping the signal with a constant intensity and changing the fluence of the amplifier. Figure 3b indicates the collected intensity as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, indicated by the blue, orange and green curves, respectively (Methods). At low pump fluences, the output signal remains unchanged, whereas at higher amplifier fluences it is strongly enhanced at 0 delay (Δt = 0 ps) and then decays within roughly 50 ps, demonstrating amplification once a sufficient particle density is reached. The decay follows a single-exponential fit with a characteristic time of 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, more than 1 order of magnitude shorter than the bare photoluminescence decay (Supplementary Fig. 16). To further explain the effect, power-dependent measurements at Δt = 0 ps were performed, as shown in Fig. 3c. Here the bottom panel represents the photoluminescence intensity generated by the off-resonant amplifier alone, which increases quadratically with pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 17), whereas the top panel corresponds to the intensity measured in the presence of both the signal and the amplifier beams, showing clear amplification with a marked threshold-like behaviour. This trend confirms optical amplification and is consistent with stimulated emission, where the probe stimulates particles from the incoherent exciton reservoir created by the amplifier, possibly assisted by acoustic phonons, recently shown to play a key role in perovskites42. The amplification threshold is found to occur at roughly Pth,Amp = 10 μJ cm−2, that is, well below the lasing threshold.

Industry observers note that a, Sketch of the integrated optical circuit used to measure polariton amplification: the off-resonant beam (amplifier) creates an exciton reservoir whereas the resonant beam (signal) excites a polariton state propagating along the waveguide. At the output grating the signal is amplified (amplified signal) thanks to stimulation from the exciton reservoir. Amplifier energy is Eamplifier = 2.58 eV in all the measurements. b, Collected intensity of the amplified signal as a function of time delay for three different amplifier fluences, 3 μJ cm−2, 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2; black dashed line indicate the exponential fit. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.31 eV. A positive Δt corresponds to the case in which the signal arrives after the non-resonant pump, allowing amplification to take place while the reservoir is present. The decay time, 20.5 ± 1.2 ps, is the average of the exponential-fit values obtained at pump fluences of 20 μJ cm−2 and 38 μJ cm−2, which yield 22.1 ± 1.4 ps and 18.8 ± 0.9 ps, respectively. c, Power-dependent measurements at time delay 0 ps. Bottom: green dots represent the intensity of the amplifier alone; top, orange dots show the intensity of the amplified signal as a function of the amplifier fluence. The signal energy is Esignal = 2.26 eV. The horizontal error bars represent the power fluctuations of the amplifier, whereas the vertical error bars reflect the standard deviation derived from the signal evaluation across slightly different spectral regions, providing an estimate of the systematic uncertainty. d, Amplification factor as a function of the signal energy for two different amplifier fluences (P1 = 25 μJ cm−2 and P2 = 35 μJ cm−2) as indicated in c by the blue and red dashed lines. The amplification closely follows the photoluminescence spectral profile, increasing with the photoluminescence intensity. The photoluminescence spectrum, shown in arbitrary units, is included for qualitative comparison.

To test the spectral efficiency, we selected two amplifier fluences (P1 and P2, blue and red dashed vertical lines in Fig. 3c), both kept between the amplification and the lasing threshold, and scanned the signal energy, keeping its fluence constant. Figure 3d highlights the amplification factor as a function of the signal energy, defined as \(A=\frac{({S}_{{\rm{out}}}-{A}_{0})}{{S}_{0}}\), where Sout is the total output signal, and A0 and S0 are the independently measured amplifier and signal contributions, respectively. Clear amplification is observed over a broad energy range, with a superlinear dependence on signal energy and increasing spectral efficiency due to more efficient scattering and reduced group velocity, which enhances the interaction time with the reservoir. Crucially, amplification is observed even at energies well outside the narrow spectral region where lasing occurs (Supplementary Fig. 18) thus ruling out a cavity-mode feeding mechanism, which would instead be confined to the narrow spectral region defined by the lasing modes. In Supplementary Fig. 19, we present representative real-space maps of the signal, the amplifier and the amplified signal. Moreover, at the highest signal energy for which propagation is still sustained in the system the amplification factor approaches two orders of magnitude. Taking into account the spatial extension of the reservoir (Supplementary Fig. 18), we estimate the optical gain within a simple one-dimensional model as g = ln(A)/L, where A is the measured amplification factor and L is the effective interaction length, approximated by the amplifier full-width at half-maximum (13–15 µm). This yields values in the range of 5 × 102–3 × 103 cm−1 depending on the signal energy. Moreover, above the lasing threshold, the amplified signal saturates (Extended Data Fig. 7), consistent with reservoir depletion induced by the self-oscillating mode. Combining room-temperature operation with liquid-phase synthesis, our results represent a great advance over GaAs-based or ZnO-based platforms, which instead require cryogenic operation and demanding epitaxial growth16,43. In addition, the strong-coupling regime enables amplification through bosonic stimulation rather than population inversion, allowing operation at lower pump powers than conventional gain media.

Industry observers note that we then exploit the complex geometries enabled by our fabrication approach to demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton system. A resonant signal beam (Eres = 2.265 eV) is injected through the input grating, propagates along the structure and is subsequently split into the two arms of an interferometric Y-splitter. At the end of each arm, the waveguide edges act as outcouplers, allowing for the formation of an interference pattern in the momentum space, directly accessing the relative phase difference between the two arms. A non-resonant pulse is then introduced in only one arm of the Y-splitter. A schematic of the configuration is shown in Fig. 4a, and the reflectivity image of the Y-splitter termination and the corresponding outcoupled signal are shown in Fig. 4b. A representative momentum-space map recorded with only the propagating signal highlights the expected interference pattern (Fig. 4c), whose origin is confirmed by selectively removing one output from the detection path (Supplementary Fig. 20). We then monitor the interference fringe shift as a function of the phase-shifter pulse energy at zero delay Δt = 0 ps between the optical shifter and the propagating signal beam. As shown in Fig. 4d, where the intensity profile along kx is plotted as a function of the optical-shifter fluence, a pronounced shift is generated. The phase shift, extracted from sinusoidal fits of the interferograms, reaches up to 2π with increasing pump pulse energy (Fig. 4e). As a consistency check, moving the phase-shifter beam to the opposite arm reverses the fringe shift direction (Extended Data Fig. 8), whereas amplification is observed only in the pumped arm (Supplementary Fig. 21). We model the experiment using two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance, as described in the Methods. At fixed probe frequency, this shift produces a change in the polariton wavevector and the corresponding phase accumulated over the propagation length is reported in Fig. 4f as a function of the exciton resonance shift.

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic of the Y-splitter device with an integrated input grating used to split a propagating resonant signal inside the structure while a non-resonant phase shifter (EPS = 2.58 eV) is applied only on one of its two arms. The ends of the two arms outcouple the propagating signal and behave as spatially separated coherent emitters, generating an interference pattern in momentum space that provides direct access to the relative phase. b, Real-space image of the Y-splitter termination (top) and the corresponding outcoupled signal (bottom) when only the resonant beam is present. c, Representative momentum-space map showing the interference pattern arising from coherent out-coupling of the two arms. d, Evolution of the interference fringes for increasing phase-shifter fluence. The direction of the fringe shift is highlighted by the black arrow. Bottom black profile represents the signal alone. Note that the incident pulse energy per operation is used here as the relevant metric (rather than fluence), as appropriate for single-device operation. The device footprint is roughly 20 μm2. e, Phase shift as a function of energy per pulse, showing a continuous increase reaching 2π. f, Calculated phase shift considering two polaritonic waveguides described by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one incorporating a small shift of the exciton resonance. Scale bars, 2 μm (b), 1.5 μm–1 (c).

Finally, after establishing the presence of a suitable π-phase shift in the Y-splitter geometry, we extend this functionality to a full Mach–Zehnder interferometer. The polariton mode is resonantly excited at 2.265 eV through the input grating, while the transmitted signal is collected at the output, with the phase shifter applied to one arm of the interferometer, as illustrated in Fig. 5a,b. The output intensity is extracted from a fixed spatial region at the grating outcoupler and is shown in Fig. 5c after background subtraction (Supplementary Fig. 22). As the phase-shifter energy increases, the signal evolves from a maximum to a minimum and then back to a maximum, demonstrating a full 2π response well reproduced by a sine-squared fit. Notably, this sizable phase shift is achieved within an ultra-compact guided footprint (roughly 20 µm2, Fig. 5b), compared with millimetre-scale lithium-niobate phase shifters44,45. The large modulation is enabled by the polaritonic nature of the guided mode that enhances the nonlinear response to the pump-induced reservoir. Beyond its compactness, the direct use of polaritonic nonlinearities, with a residual contribution from the excitonic reservoir due to the off-resonant excitation, offers a route towards ultrafast integrated circuitry compared with thermo-optic nonlinearities46,47,48.

Sources indicate that a, Microscope image of the Mach–Zehnder interferometer with an integrated input and output grating. b, Example of the experimental configuration adopted: a resonant beam with a full-width at half-maximum comparable to the size of the grating coupler is focused on the input grating (left, signal input), propagates along the structure and is outcoupled at the output grating (right, signal output). The phase-shifter beam was pumping one arm of the interferometer. The images of the signal input, phase shifter and signal output regions were acquired separately and subsequently rescaled in intensity. c, Signal output as a function of the phase-shifter energy: black dots represent the experimental data, and the red line indicates the fitted curve. The data are collected at Δt = 0 ps, corresponding to temporal synchronization between the travelling signal beam and the phase-shifter beam at the phase-shifter spatial position. Scale bars, 10 μm.

In summary, we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polariton waveguide platform operating at room temperature, combining strong nonlinear propagation, tunable polariton lasing, optical amplification and nonlinear phase control within a single device. Our approach introduces a hybrid and high-throughput soft-lithography method that combines surface-tension–guided assembly with microfluidics, enabling single-step direct fabrication of active waveguides with integrated grating couplers. This provides a straightforward, cost-effective and scalable route for realizing self-assembled complex polaritonic architectures without the need for specialized vacuum equipment or epitaxial reactors. The developed architecture supports on-chip polariton lasing, with wavelength-selective emission enabled by longitudinal feedback from the integrated gratings and efficient propagation along the waveguide. Beyond lasing, we demonstrate room-temperature amplification of guided polariton signals by nearly two orders of magnitude. The threshold-like amplification and nonlinear response suggest potential for neuromorphic polariton devices, in which tailored excitation geometries and pulse sequences could enable neuron-like operations such as signal integration and threshold-triggered emission.

In a recent development, furthermore, we demonstrate nonlinear phase control in a guided polariton configuration, achieving phase shifts exceeding π within an ultra-compact footprint. Crucially, we harness this capability in a fully integrated Mach–Zehnder interferometer, enabling direct conversion of phase modulation into intensity modulation. The ability to coherently control the phase of propagating signals, combined with intrinsic ultrafast polaritonic nonlinearities, establishes this platform as a promising route towards ultrafast on-chip interferometric devices. These features—combining room-temperature operation, material tunability, scalable and cost-effective fabrication, and rich nonlinear functionalities—establish perovskite polariton waveguides as a versatile and promising platform for next-generation integrated photonic and polaritonic technologies.

Industry observers note that the grating and waveguide nanostructures and microstructures were fabricated on 25 × 25 mm Si(100) substrates using EBL (RAITH Voyager) followed by reactive ion etching. The grating pattern was defined using a 130-nm-thick poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) electron-beam resist layer spin-coated onto the silicon substrate and exposed by EBL at a dose of 580 μC cm−2. The exposed resist was developed in a MIBK:IPA (1:3) solution. A 40-nm-thick chromium film, serving as an etch hard mask, was subsequently deposited by electron-beam evaporation, and the remaining resist was removed in acetone. The pattern was transferred for 50 nm into the silicon substrate using fluorine-based reactive ion etching (CF4, CHF3, O2, Ar). The chromium mask was then removed by wet chemical etching. An analogous process was used for the fabrication of the waveguide structures, with optimized parameters as follows: PMMA resist thickness of 360 nm, EBL exposure dose of 280 μC cm−2, chromium mask thickness of 60 nm and reactive ion etching etching depth of 250 nm. Following chromium mask removal, the silicon master was cleaned in a piranha solution for 15 min to eliminate any residual organic contamination. The final silicon master featured microwire waveguides and interferometer-like geometries with lateral dimensions from 2 µm to 30 µm, and a height of 250 nm. Each waveguide incorporated nanometre-scale grating arrays covering areas of roughly 10 × 10 µm2, with a height of 50 nm, pitches between 240 nm and 300 nm and varying filling factors, directly etched onto the surface. The aspect ratios (height/width) of the patterned structures, including both the waveguides and the gratings, ranged from approximately 0.01 to 0.60. The grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4), so that the grating lines remain confined within the inner region of the waveguide and do not overlap with the waveguide borders in the etch mask, thereby avoiding local sidewall indentations during the two-step dry-etching process and preserving a more uniform waveguide geometry for crystal growth. For the interferometer, the structure includes a sequence of lateral modulations before the Y-splitter, efficiently redistributing the guided mode into the two branches (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Perovskite devices were fabricated using a modified soft-lithography approach that combined surface-tension-driven lithography with microfluidic processing of a liquid precursor solution, using PDMS replicas moulded from silicon masters with predefined multiscale geometries. A mixture of PDMS prepolymer and curing agent (10:1, Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was cast onto the Si master and cured at 140 °C for 10 min. The polymerized PDMS layer was then carefully detached from the master before the use. A 0.42 M precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 106 mg of CsBr and 183.5 mg of PbBr2 (1:1 molar ratio) in 1.2 ml of dimethylsulfoxide. The mixture was stirred at 80 °C on a hotplate inside a nitrogen-filled glove box for 2 h, yielding a clear solution. Immediately before use, the precursor solution was diluted to concentrations in the range 0.05–0.1 M for the CsPbBr3 crystal growth. The precursor solution was deposited in contact with the patterned PDMS replica until the capillary pressure required for complete imbibition of the microstructures and nanostructures was reached. Once nucleation began, with the liquid meniscus pinned to the sidewalls of the nanoscale features, the PDMS replica was placed in conformal contact with a glass substrate to seal the microwire waveguides26,27. At this stage, capillary forces and surface interactions guided the solution through the microfluidic channels. Within the confined geometry, the reduced precursor volume and the progressively increasing concentration and viscosity gradients promoted perovskite nucleation through surface-tension-driven self-assembly precisely at the elastomer–air interface of each microstructure and nanostructure28,49,50,51. Crystallization inside the microchannels was optimized by imposing controlled temperature ramps (from 4 °C to room temperature) and by maintaining controlled vapour saturation and a pressure of 0.02 N cm−2 (refs. 52,53). After complete solvent evaporation, the PDMS replica was removed, yielding CsPbBr3 positive structures directly on the glass substrate that faithfully reproduced the microscale and nanoscale features of the original Si master. To assess fabrication reproducibility, we report in Supplementary Fig. 23 a set of nominally identical microwire arrays fabricated under the same conditions. The samples demonstrated a consistent optical response, with only minor detuning variations. It is important to note that the grating width was intentionally designed to be smaller than the waveguide width, see Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, to preserve continuous sidewalls in the elastomeric microchannels used for soft-lithography growth, ensuring uniform capillary filling and crystallization conditions while avoiding sidewall discontinuities that could introduce structural defects or make the crystal more fragile during replica peeling. The accessible limits of the proposed fabrication approach were determined by the fidelity of pattern transfer from the master mould to the elastomeric replica and subsequently to the perovskite crystal. On the basis of the aspect ratios demonstrated here (0.01–0.6), we anticipate that perovskite waveguides with thicknesses of roughly 100–150 nm and lateral dimensions of roughly 250–400 nm should be feasible. For periodic nanostructures, we note that some of the geometries investigated in this work (Supplementary Fig. 2) already contain lateral features as small as 50–80 nm, approaching the practical resolution limit of standard PDMS-based replication. Further reduction of the feature size would probably require optimization of the elastomeric replica itself.

Confocal images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope in high-resolution mode (1,024 × 1,024 pixel). Samples were prepared on microscope slides and characterized using a 488-nm excitation laser and a main beam splitter (MBS 488/639-nm) with appropriate photomultiplier tube (PMT) and gallium arsenide phosphide (GaAsP) detectors. All samples were imaged at various magnifications using Initiative-Apochromat objectives of ×10 with a numerical aperture of NA = 0.45, ×20 NA = 0.8 and ×40 NA = 0.95. Three-dimensional images were obtained using the Z-stack scanning mode, which generated optical slices at various depths. Image analysis across different acquisition channels, tomographic reconstructions, spectral profiles and three-dimensional rendering were performed using the dedicated ZEN BLUE software.

According to recent reports, AFM measurements were performed with a Dimension Icon (Bruker AXS) instrument, equipped with the Nanoscope V controller. Images were acquired in air, at room temperature, in Tapping Mode to protect the samples from damage. A rotated tapping etched silicon probe (Bruker) with a nominal radius of curvature R ≤ 8 nm was used. The morphology of the Si masters was investigated using a Sigma 300 (Zeiss) field emission SEM operated at an acceleration voltage of 5 kV and with an in-lens detector.

All the optical measurements were performed by using microscope objectives at ×100 magnification and a numerical aperture of 0.9 (Zeiss) in a reflection configuration. The pumping lasers were taken from a pulsed source (Pharos, Light Conversion) with a tunable repetition rate and a pulse duration of <290 fs, which drove two computer-controlled optical parametric amplifier (OPA) stages (Orpheus OPA, Light Conversion). The OPA outputs were independently tunable in wavelength and, depending on the specific measurement (single-beam or double-beam excitation), were used either simultaneously or individually. In all the experiments, the repetition rate was set to 10 kHz. Energy-resolved momentum-space maps were collected by imaging the back focal plane of the objective onto the entrance of a spectrometer (Andor, Kymera 328i Spectrograph), equipped with three gratings (150 lines per mm, 300 lines per mm, 600 lines per mm) and coupled to a two-dimensional charge-coupled device (CCD camera, Andor, iStar 334T). For photoluminescence off the resonance pump, the laser was set to 480 nm and the emitted photoluminescence signal was filtered using an edgepass filter (Thorlabs, FELH0500) to suppress the residual excitation laser and isolate the emission. TE and TM polarizations were defined with the waveguide axis aligned to the entrance slits of the spectrometer, such that the electric field was parallel (TE) or perpendicular (TM) to the grating periodicity. The two polarizations were selectively monitored by using a half-wave plate (AHWP10M-600) and a linear polarizer (GTH10M-A) along the detection line. The laser pumping power was controlled by using a variable neutral-density wheel filter. For double-beam experiments, the two OPA outputs were temporally matched by using a delay line (Newport, M-ILS 150CC DC Servo Linear Stage). Reflectivity measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 5 were performed by using a broadband white-light illumination in a reflection configuration, with a spot diameter of roughly 10 μm on the grating coupler. For the photoluminescence measurements shown in Supplementary Fig. 7, the waveguide was excited between two gratings whereas for Supplementary Fig. 6 the emission from a single grating was spatially selected. With reference to Fig. 3b, the temporal profiles were obtained by subtracting the residual photoluminescence signal generated by the amplifier alone, which remained constant across all temporal scans. The amplifier-only signal was collected separately using the same exposure time and then subtracted from the measurements in which both beams were simultaneously present. The same procedure was applied to the measurements in Fig. 4c,d, for which the signal obtained with the phase shifter alone was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from the corresponding datasets. For the amplification measurements, Δt = 0 ps is defined as the relative amplifier-signal delay that maximizes the amplified signal intensity at the pumped region. This delay was experimentally optimized at each amplifier power, thereby inherently accounting for the relaxation dynamics leading to the population responsible for amplification and their possible dependence on the amplifier power.

In a recent development, infinitely periodic dispersions have been calculated taking into account fully dispersive experimental literature values for the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index54. To quantitatively relate the measured phase difference to a microscopic excitonic energy shift, we consider two waveguides governed by the same light–matter coupled dispersion, with one of them subjected to a small blueshift of the exciton resonance. To relate to this experiment, this blueshift came from the interaction between the signal and the reservoir created by the non-resonant pump. The system was probed at a fixed frequency (ω), such that the effect of the perturbation would not change the frequency of the mode, but rather modify its propagation constant. The observable phase difference after a propagation length L therefore directly reflected the difference in wavevectors between the two configurations, (Δɸ = ΔkL). We consider the propagation of a waveguided mode in the strong-coupling regime described by the lower polariton dispersion relation. For a reference waveguide, the dispersion reads:.

Here k denotes the in-plane wavevector (propagation constant) of the guided mode and c represents the slope of the bare photonic dispersion, such that \({E}_{{\rm{ph}}}(k)\approx {ck}\). The parameter Ω corresponds to the Rabi splitting energy whereas ωx is the exciton resonance energy. The non-resonant pump on the second waveguide creates an exciton reservoir inducing a blueshift of the exciton, therefore the dispersion of the waveguide under the non-resonant pump reads:.

I.V. and R.M. optimized the growth process and fabricated the samples used for the optical measurements. R.M. prepared the precursor solution for perovskite growth. K.D. modelled the phase-shift experiment. E.F. and S.S. performed the AFM measurements. F.T. performed further SEM characterization. A.F. analysed the data and wrote the paper with input from all authors. D.G. and T.C.H.L. supervised the theoretical work. V.A., M.B., F.B., M.D.G., D.B. and D.S. contributed to the discussion of the data analysis and the structure of the paper. D.S. supervised the project. All authors discussed the results and contributed to the interpretation of the data and the final paper.

Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The stirring of what might yet be a great partnership between Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, although it will need to be, given some of the chaos that endures at Chelsea.
  • Recent findings suggest that this was a Premier League game played at a furious pace, and the two former Real Madrid team-mates in charge of the sides will not have seen much of the control all coaches seek.
  • That was chiefly the fault of Robert Sánchez, who was embraced afterwards by Alonso, having demonstrated just how damaging a shaky goalkeeper can be to any serious team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The stirring of what might yet be a great partnership between Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, although it will need to be, given some of the chaos that endures at Chelsea.

Recent findings suggest that this was a Premier League game played at a furious pace, and the two former Real Madrid team-mates in charge of the sides will not have seen much of the control all coaches seek. Xabi Alonso’s team eventually won with a goal from each of his attacking triumvirate of Rogers, Palmer and João Pedro – and at times it will have been painful for the new Chelsea manager.

That was chiefly the fault of Robert Sánchez, who was embraced afterwards by Alonso, having demonstrated just how damaging a shaky goalkeeper can be to any serious team. Álvaro Arbeloa’s Fulham had their moments – and the best ones were granted to them by Sánchez. At a club that is such a restless trader of footballers, it feels remarkable that Sánchez has endured for so long.

Alonso played down the significance of Sánchez’s errors, although he cannot seriously be considering sticking to his mantra of “relax and carry on”. That was, he said, his response to the first-half Sánchez mistake that let in Josh King’s shot for Fulham’s first goal. Sánchez could have done a lot better with Gonzalo García’s goal after the break.

Fulham have equalised against Chelsea thanks to Josh King's low strike 💥 pic.twitter.com/WCLKB7XqeE.

Gonzalo Garcia has scored on his Premier League debut after Robert Sanchez spilled Castagne's shot 🤯 pic.twitter.com/BmP6eqwkuN.

Chelsea have a lot of faith that Mike Penders, the 21-year-old Belgian on the bench for this game, will be their first-choice goalkeeper eventually. The situation seems rather more urgent and with Penders likely to feature against Luton Town on Thursday night in the Carabao Cup it would appear a big decision is looming for Alonso.

In terms of the Palmer-Rogers axis, this was very promising, although there was no doubting the senior figure in this. Palmer’s ball set João Pedro free in the first minute, the Brazilian lifting a well-judged nudge over Bernd Leno.

"A flying start under Xabi Alonso!" Chelsea lead against Fulham after just 31 seconds 🤯 pic.twitter.com/LrkYxOReFB.

It was Palmer who was crucial to the second for Rogers, made by Maxence Lacroix on his debut. Palmer stroked in the third on 49 minutes with the easy confidence of a man in form.

Industry observers note that A goal for Morgan Rogers on his Chelsea debut! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/hphe8y077v.

Industry observers note that "Cole Palmer back to his best!"Palmer has scored to double Chelsea's lead! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/zo6e0Vdcgq.

It has been revealed that “I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”.

Sources indicate that palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”.

According to recent reports, if there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Recent findings suggest that sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

According to recent reports, there was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

Recent findings suggest that it was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

“We concede goals in the first minute, the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half and there are not worse moments to concede. But we revealed character and personality and I am very proud of how my players responded. We deserved a little bit more but football is not about what you deserve, it is about what you take. If you lose against a team like Chelsea they [should] have to do a little bit more. For me, they are easy goals for them and mistakes we cannot make. We need to improve and be more ready in the first minute, that is for sure.

“We are on our way and we will keep improving. The first thing I want to see is a competitive team. We were tonight, we tried our best and tried to play our football against a team like Chelsea, which is not easy. I believe in them and I believe in young players. I think they have the energy and ambition I want and they fit in the way I play. Josh King is absolutely amazing. I am really happy with him. Gonzalo [Garcia] scored and Cesar [Palacios] did well. I think they need a bit more time but they are doing great and making an impact already.”.

"We need to help them, not to rely everything on them" Xabi Alonso speaking about Chelsea's 'special' front three 🔵 pic.twitter.com/JnSBoNexF4.

"Arsenal DON'T win the league if they have Ramsdale and not Raya" 🧤@Carra23 and @GNev2 think that upgrading the goalkeeper position could be the 'last piece' for Chelsea 🧩 pic.twitter.com/UBzMCFmxpp.

"You can see in his eyes, he's ready to prove people wrong""Best player on the pitch by a mile" 👏Morgan Rogers reacts to his debut and the performance of Cole Palmer pic.twitter.com/M7JKk1MQ8U.

"How ready are you?""Did you not watch the game?" 😅Cole Palmer says he is 'hungry' and ready to get back to his best! pic.twitter.com/xpg5zJl9k0.

2 - Cole Palmer tonight vs Fulham:1 goal1 assist5 dribbles completed5 shots3 chances created7 ball recoveries10 duels wonHe was only the second player on record since 2006-07 to record all of these numbers in a Premier League game.Cold. pic.twitter.com/uW4YPeHNnD.

“There were things to really like. On paper, that front three [for Chelsea] is sensational. It really is. It looked it in the game. I think Joao Pedro is fantastic. [Morgan] Rogers’ first game, what a start. But when you think of him, [Cole] Palmer and Pedro; that is as good as anything in the Premier League right now.

“But I do think concerns defensively. They conceded a couple of goals and you look at the goalkeeper. They have to sort the goalkeeper concern out because it is going to come back to haunt them this season, as it did tonight.”.

August 27: Fulham vs AFC Wimbledon (League Cup)August 30: Sunderland vs Fulham (Premier League)September 5: Fulham vs Crystal Palace (Premier League)September 12: Liverpool vs Fulham (Premier League)September 20: Fulham vs Manchester United (Premier League).

“The attacking play, Cole Palmer was sensational. If you talk about Cole Palmer getting back to his best you have got a £120m-£125m player there. [Morgan] Rogers getting a goal. Those two being electric with Joao Pedro up front. The front three were brilliant tonight. One of the best things I have seen this weekend.

Industry observers note that “They have added an experience player at centre-back, centre midfield and centre forward. I do not know if Emi Martinez is available or not but someone like that needs to come in at Chelsea, because that will undermine everything they do. The positives for Fulham came from the encouragement [Robert] Sanchez gave them with the goals. The goals were both mistakes. It is a problem.”.

Possession: Fulham 61%-39% ChelseaShots: 14-18Shots on target: 6-6Corners: 6-4Touches in opposition box: 24-38.

The final whistle is blown at Craven Cottage and Chelsea hold on to win 3-2 to give Xabi Alonso a win in his first game in charge. Alvaro Arbeloa’s first game as Fulham boss ends in defeat. An absorbing west London derby.

Garcia throws himself to the ground as Sessegnon sends in a cross but that is never going to be a penalty.

Recent findings suggest that will there be one more chance for Fulham to try and find an equaliser? Time is running out for the hosts.

Pedro has the ball in the back of the Fulham net but Quenda was offside in the build-up. A quick VAR check proves so.

There will be four added minutes.

Industry observers note that surely there is another goal in this one? It is a surprise there has not been since Garcia got a goal back for Fulham.

The latest booking of the game goes the way of Castagne, who cynically trips Colwill.

Sessegnon is played in down the left channel and flicks it past Acheampong inside the Chelsea penalty area. Sessegnon gets his shot away from a narrow angle and it is straight at Sanchez.

According to recent reports, palmer looks like he might have cramp in his calf and is going to be replaced by Estevao. Quenda also comes on for Chelsea, coming on for Rogers.

Fulham make an attacking alteration as Muniz replaces Robinson.

According to recent reports, that is a huge, huge chance for Fulham to equalise. Robinson is played in behind the Chelsea defence with a long ball in behind and Sanchez is in no-man’s land out of his goal. Robinson just has to lift it over Sanchez from the edge of the box but his effort goes wide. Fulham should be on level terms.

Fulham fans think they are about to be awarded a free-kick right outside the box but instead the free-kick goes the other way. It was a clear dive from Bassey, who is rightly booked for simulation.

James is the third Chelsea player into the book for cynically pulling King back. James then has the cheek to wag his finger at King, as if it was not a foul, yet it was a clear booking. James had to be careful there as some referees may not have taken too kindly to that.

Double change for Fulham as Kevin and Sessegnon are brought on.

Recent findings suggest that that would have been a great goal from King. He has already scored once and is inches away from his second. He receives a pass on the turn from Robinson and drives towards the Chelsea box. He then cuts inside onto his right, beating Lacroix with ease, and nearly beats Sanchez at his near post but his shot goes inches wide.

This is a very open, end-to-end game and you would fully expect more goals in this one. I would be very surprised if this one ended 3-2. Both defences are looking leaky.

Fulham are going to make their substitution of the night as Charles comes on for his debut having signed from Southampton, replacing Bobb.

Enzo is being booed a lot by the home fans every time he touches the ball.

It has been revealed that chelsea are the first to turn to their bench. Enzo is coming on and is met by a lot of boos, mostly though from the home fans as the majority of the travelling Chelsea fans are applauding him. Chavarria is also on to make his Chelsea debut. Hato and Lavia head off.

According to recent reports, there is a fresh rule being implemented. Hato takes far too long over a throw-in and Fulham are therefore awarded the throw-in instead.

It has been revealed that when Palmer put Chelsea 3-1 up, the visitors looked in control of this match. Fast forward five minutes and the momentum has completely switched around. What an absorbing opening Monday night of the season!

The Fulham debutant gives them life and this game is not over. Castagne is found making a run in behind and cuts back inside onto his left inside the Chelsea penalty area. His shot is straight at Sanchez, who can only parry it straight into the path of Garcia, who heads into the ground and the ball bounces over Sanchez into the Chelsea net. Another poor piece of goalkeeping from Sanchez.

Gonzalo Garcia has scored on his Premier League debut after Robert Sanchez spilled Castagne's shot 🤯 pic.twitter.com/BmP6eqwkuN.

All members of Chelsea’s starting front three have got on the scoresheet tonight and Palmer also has an assist to his name.

Chelsea come close to a fourth as Hato squares it for Rogers inside the Fulham box but Robinson nips in just in front to clear.

He came close to scoring moments ago and now he does get on the scoresheet. Pedro gets onto the end of a flicked-on header by Rogers near halfway and drives into the Fulham half. As he gets to the Fulham penalty area, he waits for the overlapping run of Palmer and times the pass just right. Palmer, from a narrow angle, puts it between Leno’s legs and into the far corner.

"Cole Palmer back to his best!"Palmer has scored to double Chelsea's lead! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/zo6e0Vdcgq.

In a recent development, palmer does brilliantly down Chelsea’s right to skip past a number of defenders and moves into the Fulham penalty area. He opens up his body and curls one towards the far corner. He is adamant that there is a deflection but a goal kick is given. Replays show Palmer may have had a point.

We are back under way at Craven Cottage.

Nottingham Forest are ramping up their pursuit of Chelsea’s Liam Delap as Oliver Glasner eyes two major signings before the window closes.

Forest are in talks with Chelsea over a potential loan deal for the forward after he was made available at Stamford Bridge and not included in their opening-day squad against Fulham.

Negotiations are ongoing, but Delap fits the profile of striker Forest are prioritising and is a long-term target for both the club and Glasner from his spell at Crystal Palace.

Possession: Fulham 60%-40% ChelseaShots: 7-13Shots on target: 2-5Corners: 4-3Touches in opposition box: 16-18.

In a recent development, an absorbing first half at Craven Cottage is brought to a close and Chelsea take a 2-1 lead into the break. Pedro put them ahead inside the first minute before King equalised for Fulham. However Rogers, on his Chelsea debut, put the visitors back in front not long before half-time.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Palmer, who has run the show for Chelsea in this first half, is inches away from putting the visitors 3-1 up. Both sides have been guilty of giving the ball away in dangerous areas and Fulham do so on this occasion. Palmer then curls an effort from the edge of the box but his shot goes just wide of the far post.

The British record transfer puts Chelsea back in front on his official debut. It stems from great play from centre-back Lacroix, who finds himself in an advanced position and receives a pass from Palmer on the right side of the box. Lacroix cuts it across to Rogers, who makes no mistake from 12 yards out. Assist and goal both coming from fresh signings.

A goal for Morgan Rogers on his Chelsea debut! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/hphe8y077v.

Fulham fail to clear a cross from James into their box and Hato’s header falls at the feet of Lavia, whose shot from close range is saved by Leno.

According to recent reports, is Colwill lucky to still be on the pitch? The ball is played in behind the Chelsea defence and Colwill appeared to throw his arm across King but no foul is given. That could so easily have been given as a free-kick and a second yellow card.

Industry observers note that rogers drives towards the Fulham box and cuts inside onto his right foot. His effort is blocked by Cuenca before James’ first-time shot is straight at Leno.

In a recent development, chelsea are inches from going back in front. It stems from great work from Palmer, who drives down Chelsea’s right. His cross from the right side of the box picks out Pedro near the penalty spot. The Brazilian volleys it first time but his effort goes just wide.

Fulham are on top at the moment and Chelsea are lucky shaky as they are under the cosh inside their own box. King is playing really well, finding pockets of space down Fulham’s right and looking a real threat.

According to recent reports, fulham are back on level terms but it is really poor goalkeeping from Sanchez. King, who had just threatened down Fulham’s right, receives a pass from Castagne on the right touchline and takes a touch into the Chelsea box. King then fires his shot away at the near post and gets plenty of power on it but there is no way Sanchez should be beaten. He is beaten and Fulham equalise. Good strike from King but terrible keeping from Sanchez.

Fulham have equalised against Chelsea thanks to Josh King's low strike 💥 pic.twitter.com/WCLKB7XqeE.

According to recent reports, chelsea haven’t spent all that money on Rogers for his defending, but Alonso won’t have liked the way he let Josh King to run past him to collect the ball and smash Fulham level. Rogers switched off there.

King does brilliantly to drive down Fulham’s right and flashes a dangerous ball across the six-yard box but none of his teammates are on hand to meet the cross.

Fulham are flirting with danger in and around their box and are a touch fortunate not to concede a second goal.

Down the other end, King is urged to shoot from outside the box and he obliges. It looks like it should be a fairly routine save for Sanchez but the Chelsea keeper looks uncomfortable and pushes it behind for a corner. The delivery comes to the near post and King, who lays it off the edge of the box. It comes to Palacios, who cannot guide his effort on target.

Chelsea started this game well but have lost control and are asking for trouble. The latest example sees Sanchez take too long to clear and he accidentally allows the ball to go out before clearing to gift Fulham a corner. Bobb’s delivery is headed away at the near post by James.

Sources indicate that that is strong one-vs-one defending from Bassey. Palmer lifts the ball over the top to pick out the run of Pedro, who is dispossessed inside the Fulham box by Bassey.

Moments later, Lavia flies into a reckless challenge on Bassey and is booked. Lavia looks stunned at that decision but he is perhaps on the fortunate side that VAR did not advise the referee to have a further look at that on the screen. Lavia was out of control and could have easily been in more trouble. Two Chelsea players already into the book and were a little bit lucky.

Palmer had just one Premier League assist to his name throughout last season and has already matched that tally tonight on the opening weekend.

Colwill is in trouble. Could Chelsea go down to 10 men early? He loses possession poorly inside his own half and then resorts to hacking Bobb down with a nasty challenge. Was Colwill the last man and could Bobb have gone racing in on goal? Colwill is booked and is perhaps a touch fortunate, although what saved him is that you perhaps could not definitively say that it was a denial of a goal-scoring opportunity.

How do Alvaro Arbeloa and his Fulham side react now they are a goal down early?

With their first attack of the Xabi Alonso era, Chelsea hit the front inside the opening minute of this west London derby. Lacroix’s header from halfway finds Palmer, who plays it into the path of Pedro. The Brazilian, fresh from signing a new deal at the club, takes it in his stride and, from inside the Fulham penalty area, lifts it over Leno and into the far corner. A fine finish from Pedro and Alonso has the perfect start.

"A flying start under Xabi Alonso!" Chelsea lead against Fulham after just 31 seconds 🤯 pic.twitter.com/LrkYxOReFB.

It has been revealed that could Joao Pedro be the man to finally lift the curse of the number nine shirt at Chelsea? Liam Delap tried and failed last season. Pedro has taken it this term and has started like a train with that early goal. Pedro has also been prolific in pre-season and has been widely tipped to be one of the Premier League’s top scorers.

Before we get going, we take a moment to remember the great Kevin Keegan, who managed Fulham in the late 1990s.

We are under way at Craven Cottage in the final game on this opening weekend of the upcoming Premier League season.

Alvaro Arbeloa is out on the pitch for the first time in the Premier League. A friendly if not rapturous welcome from the home fans. He’s rolled his sleeves up and he’s ready to go - literally, his skinny fit jacket has sleeves rolled up tight. It looks quite uncomfortable.

Industry observers note that it might be a fresh season and a new manager, but Chelsea are still doing their pre-match huddle. Fortunately, it was nowhere near the referee or the centre circle. It seemed to be captain Reece James doing all the talking.

In a recent development, both sides emerge from the tunnel at Craven Cottage and we are moments away from kick-off in this west London derby. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up tonight:.

Fulham: Leno; Castagne, Cuenca, Bassey, Robinson, King, Berge, Iwobi; Bobb, Garcia, Palacios.Substitutes: Lecomte, De Gougerolles, Tete, Reed, Charles, Sessegnon, Kevin, Smith Rowe, Muniz.

Chelsea: Sanchez; Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill; Gusto, Lavia, James, Hato; Palmer, Pedro, Rogers.Substitutes: Penders, Chavarria, Barco, Enzo, Neto, Gittens, Estevao, Welbeck, Quenda.

The boos for Fernandez from the Fulham fans got a lot louder when the players stepped on the pitch. Some people chanted something rather nasty beginning with ‘w’ as well.

Sources indicate that there were a few boos from the Fulham fans when Enzo Fernandez’s name was read out ahead of kick-off. Clearly the England fans at Craven Cottage haven’t forgotten what happened against Argentina. Fernandez was booed by some Chelsea supporters in pre-season, but there were no loud jeers from the away end during the team announcements.

Recent findings suggest that “During the week they had a few setbacks. With Moises [Caicedo], and with any [player], we do not want to take too much risk. They were not ready to play tonight. We need to go week-by-week but for tonight they were not ready.”.

Chelsea certainly have an army of staff. I just counted 13 staff members helping the players through their warm-up. One of them is the latest set-piece coach Austin MacPhee, who is carrying around a clipboard, presumably with all his set-piece tricks on it. Culture guru Willi Isa is also out there, as is former interim manager Calum McFarlane.

Two former Liverpool, Real Madrid and Spain teammates go head-to-head in the dugouts at Craven Cottage as Fulham host Chelsea in a west London derby to round out the opening weekend of the upcoming Premier League season. Alvaro Arbeloa and Xabi Alonso were teammates at Liverpool, Real Madrid and Spain and both had stints as Real Madrid manager last season but have new homes in London. Arbeloa has replaced Marco Silva, who is now at Benfica, whilst Alonso is Liam Rosenior’s permanent replacement. This is the first time a manager’s Premier League debut has come against someone he also played alongside in the competition.

According to recent reports, “I know Alonso well because I have watched so many games of his teams,” Arbeloa said. “We have to be ready, and if we want to beat them we will have to play very well. I spoke to Xabi a few days ago. But not about football; both of our families are coming to London, and we are very good friends, until Monday night [tonight]. We will be there on the touchline, so close for 90 minutes, and we will give everything for our clubs. For those 90 minutes, we are not friends.”.

Arbeloa has gone back to his former club to add a couple of players in the shape of Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios. The opening weekend has not served Fulham well of late; they have won just one of their last six Premier League opening weekend fixtures. They concluded their pre-season with a 1-0 win over Stuttgart.

Chelsea have been very active in the transfer market this summer, breaking the British transfer record to sign Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa as well as adding experience through the likes of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, whilst the likes of Marc Cucurella, Andrey Santos and Trevoh Chalobah have moved on. They finished off their pre-season with a 3-1 victory over Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge just over a week ago.

Recent findings suggest that “We feel ready,” Alonso stated. “We have prepared the whole pre-season with some players from the first day, other ones coming later, but the desire, the ambition, the hunger to start the Premier League is already in the building each training [session] and we are looking forward to it.”.

Enzo Fernandez has been strongly linked with a move away this summer, with Manchester City’s interest well-known.

“Enzo is a Chelsea player,” Alonso added. “He is a top, top player. He is training really well since he started 10 days ago with the team, very integrated. We are happy with him and he is getting ready for Monday. He is training really well, good attitude and that is what we want. He is trying his best to prepare for the kick-off of the Premier League.”.

Industry observers note that these sides finished on the same number of points (52) last season, with Chelsea finishing ahead on goal difference. It was one win apiece for each club in the two Premier League meetings last season. Nearly a year ago, Chelsea won 2-0 at Stamford Bridge whilst Fulham won 2-1 in this fixture at Craven Cottage back in January. Chelsea have won six of the past eight Premier League meetings at Craven Cottage.

Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Michael Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.

The Red Devils captain was also dropped for a game after publicly criticising Carrick’s tactics following a heavy Champions League defeat to Como.

The arrival of Mauricio Pochettino represents a fresh start for Fernandes this season, but there remains uncertainty over his long-term future at the club given the 32-year-old is out of contract at the end of the season.

Fernandes has already turned down two contract offers from the club, and former Brighton striker Murray believes he could be eyeing up a move away from Old Trafford when the transfer window reopens in January.

In a recent development, ‘I wouldn’t burst the bank [on a new contract] for him,’ Murray told Sky Sports. ‘I think he’s not the future of the football club.

‘Listen, he’s given his best years to Manchester United and unfortunately they haven’t won an awful lot, which he would have liked.

‘I think if he gets the option to move on, and it gets to January, and he can start speaking to other people, I think it will open his eyes up to see where he could go and if he could win things and finish off his career more enjoyably, because there have been years at Manchester United that have been really difficult.

‘He has been the standout player, but he is not the future and it could be time to part ways.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Calvert-Lewin believes Chelsea’s players could not handle the ‘intensity’ during Leeds United’s 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Chelsea took the lead in the first half through an excellent finish from Emmanuel Emegha but Xabi Alonso’s side were in front for just three minutes as Noah Okafor pulled Leeds level.

Leeds then came out flying in the second half and Leeds were given a penalty after Jayden Bogle’s thumping strike hit Rogers on the top of his arm.

Calvert-Lewin converted the spot-kick to put Leeds ahead and Daniel Farke’s side continued their dominance in the second half as Okafor netted his second of the game before Brenden Aaronson completed the deserved victory with a goal in injury time.

Chelsea have now been beaten in three out of their last four Premier League games, while only Coventry City, Ipswich Town and Crystal Palace have conceded more goals than Xabi Alonso’s side this season.

During his post-match interview with Sky Sports, Calvert-Lewin was asked what the message was from Farke during the half-time break with Chelsea already showing signs of fragility.

According to recent reports, ‘The message was just more of the same. I think we were going well, we just weren’t putting our chances away and we knew the next chance was coming and we’d have to take it,’ Calvert-Lewin replied.

‘To be honest, I expected Chelsea to come out with a bit more oomph in the second half but I think our intensity, the way that we played and the way we set up against them, they couldn’t handle it, and I think that reflected in the scoreline.’.

Asked what the message was ahead of the game against Chelsea, Calvert-Lewin replied: ‘Intensity, bring the intensity from the start.

‘We went in there with total freedom to go and play our game and just get in their face, just press, press, press. I think you could see that’s what we did and executed the gameplan well.’.

Emotional Mauricio Pochettino gets perfect sendoff in his US farewell... before boarding jet for newly introduced life as Manchester United manager
